decks.name: Machine learning concepts
cards: Overfitting
The model fits noise in the training data and generalises badly to new data.
Sign: training loss keeps falling while validation loss rises.
Underfitting
The model is too simple (or under-trained) to capture the pattern, so it does badly even on the training data.
Bias–variance trade-off
Bias is error from overly simple assumptions; variance is error from sensitivity to the particular training set. More flexibility lowers bias but raises variance.
Regularisation
Anything that discourages an overly complex model: L1/L2 penalties, dropout, early stopping, data augmentation.
L2 regularisation (weight decay)
Adds the sum of squared weights to the loss, shrinking weights towards zero.
L1 (lasso) adds absolute values instead and tends to produce sparse weights.
Gradient descent
Repeatedly step the parameters against the gradient of the loss: θ ← θ − η∇L.
Learning rate
The step size in gradient descent. Too high: oscillation or divergence. Too low: very slow, may stall.
Mini-batch gradient descent
Estimate the gradient from a random subset of the data at each step: cheaper, noisier updates that often generalise better.
Backpropagation
Computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight by applying the chain rule backwards through the network.
Chain rule
d/dx f(g(x)) = f′(g(x)) · g′(x). The mathematical basis of backpropagation.
Loss function
A number measuring how wrong the predictions are; training minimises it.
MSE for regression, cross-entropy for classification.
Cross-entropy loss
−Σ y·log(p): heavily penalises giving low probability to the true class. The standard classification loss.
Softmax
Turns a vector of scores into probabilities that are positive and sum to 1: e^zᵢ / Σⱼ e^zⱼ.
Logits
The raw, unnormalised scores a model outputs before softmax or sigmoid.
Sigmoid
σ(x) = 1 / (1 + e^−x). Squashes any value into (0, 1); used for binary probabilities.
ReLU
max(0, x). Cheap and doesn't saturate for positive inputs; long the default hidden activation.
Risk: 'dead' units that always output 0.
Why do networks need non-linear activations?
Without them, stacked linear layers collapse into one linear layer, so the network could only learn linear functions.
Vanishing gradients
Gradients shrink as they flow back through many layers (e.g. saturating sigmoids), so early layers barely learn.
Helped by ReLU, residual connections, good initialisation and normalisation.
Exploding gradients
Gradients grow exponentially through the layers and training becomes unstable.
Helped by gradient clipping and careful initialisation.
Batch normalisation
Normalises a layer's inputs over the mini-batch, then rescales with learned parameters; stabilises and speeds up training.
Layer normalisation
Normalises across the features of a single example rather than across the batch. Standard in transformers.
Dropout
Randomly zeroes a fraction of activations during training so units can't co-adapt. A regulariser; switched off at inference.
Early stopping
Stop training when validation loss stops improving, before the model overfits.
Train / validation / test split
Train fits the parameters; validation tunes hyperparameters and picks models; test is used once, at the end, to estimate real-world performance.
Cross-validation
Split the data into k folds; train on k−1 and validate on the remaining one, rotating through all folds, then average. Useful when data is scarce.
Data leakage
Information from outside the training set (test data, or the target itself) sneaks into training, giving unrealistically good results.
Precision
TP / (TP + FP): of everything flagged positive, the share that really was.
Recall
TP / (TP + FN): of all the real positives, the share you found.
F1 score
The harmonic mean of precision and recall: 2PR / (P + R).
ROC AUC
The probability that a random positive is scored higher than a random negative. 0.5 is chance; 1.0 is perfect ranking.
Confusion matrix
A table of predicted vs actual classes: counts of true/false positives and negatives.
Class imbalance
When one class is rare, accuracy misleads (always predicting 'no' can score 99%). Use precision/recall, resampling or class weights.
Supervised vs unsupervised learning
Supervised learns from labelled examples (input → target); unsupervised finds structure in unlabelled data, e.g. clustering or dimensionality reduction.
Self-supervised learning
The labels come from the data itself, e.g. predict the next token or a masked patch. How most large language models are pretrained.
Reinforcement learning
An agent learns a policy by acting in an environment and maximising cumulative reward.
k-means
Clusters data into k groups by alternating two steps: assign each point to its nearest centroid, then move each centroid to the mean of its points.
k-nearest neighbours
Predict from the labels of the k closest training examples. No training step, but prediction gets slower as the data grows.
Decision tree
Splits the data with a series of if/else questions on features. Easy to interpret, prone to overfitting.
Random forest
Many decision trees trained on random subsets of the data and features, averaging their votes (bagging) to reduce variance.
Gradient boosting
Builds models one after another, each fitting the errors (the negative gradient of the loss) of the ensemble so far.
XGBoost and LightGBM are popular implementations.
Linear regression
Fits y ≈ w·x + b by minimising squared error; has a closed-form solution (the normal equations).
Logistic regression
A linear model followed by a sigmoid, giving a probability. Despite the name, it's used for classification.
PCA
Projects data onto the directions of greatest variance (the principal components) to reduce dimensionality.
Curse of dimensionality
As the number of dimensions grows, data becomes sparse and distances less meaningful, so you need far more data.
Embedding
A learned dense vector for an item (word, image, user) such that similar items end up close together.
Cosine similarity
(a·b) / (‖a‖‖b‖): the cosine of the angle between two vectors. Ignores magnitude; widely used to compare embeddings.
Convolution (in a CNN)
Slides a small learned filter over the input, reusing the same weights everywhere, so it detects local patterns wherever they appear.
Pooling
Downsamples feature maps (e.g. the max over each 2×2 window) to shrink them and add some translation invariance.
Recurrent neural network
Processes a sequence step by step, carrying a hidden state forward. Struggles with long-range dependencies; largely replaced by transformers.
Attention
Each position takes a weighted average of other positions' values, with weights from query–key similarity: softmax(QKᵀ/√d)·V.
Self-attention
Attention where the queries, keys and values all come from the same sequence, so every token can look at every other token.
Why divide by √d in attention?
Dot products grow with the dimension d, which pushes softmax into saturated regions with tiny gradients. Scaling keeps them well-behaved.
Transformer
A stack of self-attention and feed-forward blocks, with residual connections and layer norm. The basis of modern LLMs.
Introduced in 'Attention Is All You Need' (2017).
Positional encoding
Information added to token embeddings so a transformer, which has no built-in sense of order, knows where each token sits.
Tokenisation
Splitting text into units (tokens), often sub-words from schemes like BPE, which the model maps to integer IDs.
Pretraining vs fine-tuning
Pretraining learns general representations from huge unlabelled data; fine-tuning adapts the model to a specific task with a smaller dataset.
Transfer learning
Reusing a model trained on one task as the starting point for another, saving data and compute.
Temperature (sampling)
Scales the logits before softmax: low values make output more deterministic, high values more random.
Perplexity
The exponential of the average negative log-likelihood per token. Lower means the language model is less surprised by the text.
RLHF
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: train a reward model on human preference comparisons, then optimise the language model against it.
Hallucination
When a generative model produces fluent but false or unsupported content.
Context window
The maximum number of tokens a model can take into account at once (prompt and output together).
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
Look up relevant documents (often by embedding similarity) and put them in the prompt so the model can answer from them.
Diffusion model
Learns to reverse a gradual noising process. Generation starts from pure noise and denoises step by step.
GAN
A generator tries to fool a discriminator, which tries to tell real from fake; the two are trained against each other.
Autoencoder
A network that compresses its input to a small latent code and then reconstructs it, learning a useful representation.
KL divergence
Measures how one probability distribution differs from another. Not symmetric. Appears in VAEs and RL.
Maximum likelihood estimation
Choose the parameters that make the observed data most probable. Minimising cross-entropy is MLE for classification.
Bayes' theorem
P(A|B) = P(B|A) · P(A) / P(B): how to update a belief in light of evidence.
Adam optimiser
Gradient descent with a per-parameter adaptive step size, from running averages of the gradient and its square (momentum plus RMSProp).
Momentum
Keeps a running average of past gradients so updates keep moving in consistent directions and noise averages out.
Weight initialisation
Initial weights must break symmetry and keep activations and gradients at a sensible scale: Xavier/Glorot for tanh and sigmoid, He for ReLU.
Residual connection
Adds a layer's input to its output (y = x + F(x)), giving gradients a direct path and making very deep networks trainable.
Hyperparameter
A setting chosen before training (learning rate, number of layers, regularisation strength), as opposed to parameters learned from data.
Epoch, batch, iteration
An epoch is one pass over the training set; a batch is the samples used for one update; an iteration is one update.

config.label: Explain it
lines: Explain backpropagation in two sentences without using the word 'gradient'.
Your validation loss is far above your training loss. What do you check first?
Sketch sigmoid, tanh and ReLU from memory. Where does each saturate?
Pick a paper abstract from today's reading and restate it in plain language.
Derive the gradient of mean squared error for linear regression with a single weight.
Write softmax in numpy. Why do you subtract the max before exponentiating?
Explain precision versus recall to a friend using a spam filter.
Why do we shuffle the training data between epochs?
What does learning-rate warmup do, and when would you use it?
Draw one transformer block. Which connections are residual?
Compute the cross-entropy loss for probabilities (0.7, 0.2, 0.1) when the true class is the first one.
Why use embeddings rather than one-hot vectors for words?
What does a confusion matrix tell you that accuracy doesn't?
How would you detect data leakage in a project you've been handed?
Explain how dropout behaves differently at training time and inference time.
When would you pick gradient boosting over a neural network for tabular data?
What is the difference between a loss function and an evaluation metric?
Explain the bias–variance trade-off using polynomial curve fitting.
